control_title: Encryption policy, standards, procedures and guidelines
implementation_description: The MIG Encryption Standard: TLS 1.2+ in transit, BitLocker and FileVault at rest, keys held by Information Security.
Retention schedules exist for HR, finance and health records; most other systems keep data indefinitely.
Personal data is flagged in the information asset register and handled under the Data Protection (Misty Isles) Law.
No data leakage prevention. Data exfiltration is countered only by access control and network monitoring.
Personal devices may not access or store MIG information; Entra ID conditional access allows only managed devices.

justification: MIG does not permit personal devices (DCH-12), so it never controls one.

implementation_description: ME End-Point Central reports configuration drift on Windows; Linux, OT and network devices are not checked against a baseline.
CrowdStrike Falcon prevention on IT endpoints and servers; Defender for Servers in Azure.
USB storage is blocked by CrowdStrike device control except on approved devices.
Laptops and phones are enrolled in Intune: PIN lock, remote wipe and encryption.
Screens lock after 10 minutes under the hardening standard; laptops are encrypted with BitLocker or FileVault.
The InfoSec Team scans the internal and DMZ zones monthly; OT networks are not scanned for fear of disruption.
The MIG Vulnerability Management Procedure sets patch targets by severity: critical in 14 days.
A vulnerability that cannot be fixed in time is raised as a risk; the Prison Management System exception is the example.
Every person has one named account in Active Directory and Entra ID; shared accounts are not issued.
Service accounts in Active Directory have owners; OT and appliance accounts are not recorded centrally.
Active Directory and Entra ID accounts can be listed by person; local accounts on OT systems and SaaS accounts cannot.
The MIG Access Control Policy.
Access is requested through the IT service desk and approved by the line manager and system owner.
Administrators use separate admin accounts; there is no privileged access management tool and admin sessions are not recorded.
Accounts unused for 45 days are disabled automatically; system owners do not yet review access each year.
Finance and payroll approvals require a second person; administrators cannot approve their own changes.
Remote access only through the GlobalProtect VPN from managed devices.
Administrative tools are installed only on administrators' devices.
People have one identity across Active Directory and Entra ID; OT and some SaaS accounts use other names.
Role groups in Active Directory for the main departments; many systems still grant access person by person.
The MIG Detective Monitoring Standard sets what is monitored and how the InfoSec Team handles alerts.
Security events from Windows, Linux, network appliances and Microsoft 365 are logged to Wazuh.
No application-specific logging has been defined; only platform logs are collected.
Systems synchronise with the MIG domain controllers, which take time from GPS.
CrowdStrike Falcon on IT devices and the Wazuh agent on OT detect malicious code.
The MIG Backup Policy: daily backups by Veeam, Azure Backup and Microsoft 365 Backup, kept 35 days.
Recovery objectives are set for the critical national systems; most others have none.
Quarterly phishing simulations; reported phishing goes to the InfoSec Team.
Completion of the annual training is recorded but not followed up.
Baseline personnel checks for all staff and contractors; enhanced checks for Justice and Health.
The MIG Disciplinary Procedure covers breaches of security policy.
HR notifies IT of leavers and movers; accounts are disabled on the last day.
Cloud services are assessed under the third party information risk policy; the Azure tenant follows the MIG Azure baseline.
Suppliers reach MIG systems through the VPN with their own accounts; their access is not limited to the systems they support.
Supplier VPN sessions are logged to Wazuh, but nobody reviews them.
Security requirements are agreed for major procurements; small in-house changes have none.
The small Communications development team follows OWASP guidance; there is no agreed coding standard.
In-house software is not security tested before release.
Development and test run in separate Azure subscriptions from live.
Source code is held in Azure DevOps with reviewed pull requests.
Dependencies are pinned but not scanned for known vulnerabilities.
Changes to live go through the MIG Change Advisory Board.
Contracts for bespoke development include security clauses; delivered code is not reviewed.
Staff report suspected incidents to the IT service desk or the InfoSec Team mailbox.
The incident response plan was exercised once, two years ago.
An external penetration test of the internet-facing services each year; internal systems are not tested.
Tests are scoped and authorised by the CISO before they start.
An independent review by the Island Audit Office is scheduled for next year.
Compliance is checked through this register and the SWG; there is no audit programme.
The MIG Network Security Architecture: internal, DMZ, OT and Azure zones.
Devices are not authenticated when they connect to the network.
Internal, DMZ and Azure are separated by the Palo Alto firewalls; some OT systems share the internal network.
DNS, NTP and DHCP are run by Communications and hardened under the network standard.
Staff Wi-Fi uses WPA3-Enterprise with Entra ID; guest Wi-Fi is separate from MIGNet.
Palo Alto URL filtering and DNS security; Microsoft Defender for Office 365 filters email.
No volumetric monitoring of network traffic.
Network devices are managed over SSH and HTTPS, but from ordinary desktops rather than dedicated admin devices.

MIG Official Premises and the server rooms have controlled perimeters.
Server rooms are restricted to named IT staff, with rules posted at the door.
Bank Street and Shark Point have UPS and generators; The Castle server room has UPS only.
Cabling runs in locked risers and trunking.
Equipment is maintained under supplier contracts; disks are removed before equipment leaves site.
Screens lock automatically; there is no clear desk policy.
Laptops are encrypted and staff are briefed on working off-site.
